title: Longest Increasing Subsequence II
description: Brute force to optimized: the classic O(n squared) LIS DP versus a value-indexed segment tree answering the range-max transition in O(log maxValue).

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the length of the longest subsequence of nums that is strictly increasing, and where any two consecutive elements in that subsequence differ by at most k.

blocks.text: Find the longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums where, additionally, any two consecutive chosen elements differ by no more than k.

blocks.title: Analogy: Climbing Stepping Stones That Can't Be Too Far Apart
blocks.text: Picture crossing a river on stepping stones, where each stone shows a number, and needing the longest path of strictly increasing numbers, with the added rule that any two consecutive stones stepped on cannot differ in value by more than k, limiting how big a jump is allowed.

blocks.caption: dp indexed by value: dp[num] = 1 + the best dp value in [num-k, num-1]

blocks.text: The subsequence 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 (or similar) is strictly increasing with every consecutive gap at most 3, giving a length of 5.

Before applying the classic O(n squared) LIS dynamic programming directly, notice that indexing the DP by VALUE, rather than array position, turns the transition into a range-max query, answerable efficiently with a segment tree.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Define dp[v] as the length of the best valid subsequence that ends with the value v.

Observation 2: For the current number, num, its dp value is 1 plus the maximum dp value among all values in the range [num minus k, num minus 1], since any of those could be the previous element in the subsequence.

Observation 3: A plain array scan for this range-max would still cost O(k) or O(n) per element, giving O(n squared) overall, no better than the classic LIS DP.

Observation 4: A segment tree over the VALUE range (indexed by value, not array position) supports both this range-max query and updating dp[num] after processing it, both in O(log maxValue).
This leads to a value-indexed segment tree: for each num in nums, query the maximum dp value in [num minus k, num minus 1], set dp[num] to 1 plus that, and update the segment tree at position num.
Use the classic O(n squared) LIS dynamic programming, adapted to also check the "gap at most k" condition.

items: For each index i, consider every earlier index j.
If nums[j] is less than nums[i] and nums[i] minus nums[j] is at most k, dp[i] can be dp[j] plus 1.
Take the maximum dp[i] over all valid j, and the overall answer is the maximum dp value across all i.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every earlier index is checked directly for every current index, exactly the classic O(n squared) LIS DP, with an extra gap condition.
This does not use the fact that only VALUES within k of the current one are ever relevant, checking all earlier indices regardless of their value.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the classic LIS DP complexity.
Space: O(n) for the dp array.
Limitation: with n up to 10000, O(n squared) is 100 million operations, likely too slow; the DP transition should be reformulated to use a fast range query instead of scanning every earlier element.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning every earlier element is wasteful: only elements with VALUES in [num minus k, num minus 1] are ever relevant to extending a subsequence ending at num, not every earlier array position regardless of value.

What structure supports fast value-range queries: a segment tree indexed by VALUE (not array position), storing the best dp value achieved so far for each value, supporting range-max queries and point updates.

How the DP transition becomes a query: for the current num, query the segment tree for the maximum dp value in [num minus k, num minus 1]; the current element's dp value is 1 plus that (or just 1 if the range is empty).

The core idea: process nums left to right, querying and then updating a value-indexed segment tree, giving O(log maxValue) per element.

Build a segment tree over the range of possible values. For each num in nums, in order, query the segment tree for the maximum stored value in [num minus k, num minus 1] (clamped to valid bounds); set the current subsequence length to 1 plus that query result, track the overall best length, and update the segment tree at position num with this length (if it improves the stored value there).

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: value-indexed segment tree, range-max query then point update per element

blocks.text: Indexing the DP by value, rather than array position, means "the best subsequence length ending in a value within k of num" is exactly a range-max query over [num minus k, num minus 1] in this value-indexed structure. A segment tree supports both this range-max query and the point update (recording the newly computed length at position num) in O(log maxValue), replacing the O(n) or O(k) scan the naive DP would need.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log maxValue), one query and one update per element.
Space: O(maxValue) for the segment tree.

blocks.text: Longest Increasing Subsequence II shows how indexing a DP by VALUE instead of array position can turn an O(n) or O(k) scan into an O(log maxValue) segment tree range query, a powerful and reusable technique whenever a DP transition depends on a range of values rather than a range of positions.

items: Indexing the segment tree by array position instead of by VALUE, which would not correctly support the "value within k" range query.
Forgetting to clamp the query range to valid bounds (not going below 0) when num is smaller than k.

blocks.text: Explaining why the DP is indexed by VALUE rather than position, and how that transforms the transition into a segment tree range-max query, demonstrates a strong understanding of this less common but powerful technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "n squared is too slow here", think: index the DP by value instead of position, and use a segment tree for the range-max transition.

Any DP problem where indexing by value (with a segment tree) replaces indexing by position (with a plain array scan).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized value-indexed segment tree approach runs in O(n log maxValue) time. Space is O(n) for the brute force and O(maxValue) for the optimized approach.

items: Pattern: a DP indexed by value, using a segment tree for range-max transitions instead of a plain array scan.
Core Idea: maintain the best subsequence length ending in each value, in a segment tree indexed by value; for each num, query the max in [num-k, num-1], add 1, and update the tree at num.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log maxValue) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(maxValue) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: indexing the DP by value, not array position, turns the transition into a value-range query, answerable with a segment tree.
Interview Difficulty: a strong signal problem for recognizing value-indexed DP with segment tree acceleration.
One line memory trick: DP indexed by value, segment tree range-max for the transition.
